what: Reconciliation of the seed's six largest-N rows (and its two anomalous rows) against the primary studies those rows cite. Machine-checkable companion to research/mcr-colistin-primary-studies.md.
method: PMID pulls via scripts/mcr_colistin_primary_pull.py (raw records in research/mcr-colistin-primary-raw.json); where the primary is open access, the full text was fetched from Europe PMC's fullTextXML endpoint so a table number could be checked against the table, not the abstract alone.

rows.study: Liu Y-Y, Wang Y, Walsh TR, et al. Lancet Infect Dis 2016;16(2):161-168
rows.verdict: matches exactly (the seed row is the sum of three primary sub-populations)

rows.study: Chen X, Zhao X, Che J, et al. J Med Microbiol 2017;66(2):119-125

primary.evidence: abstract: 54 (2.3%) of 2330 isolates from 10 species were mcr-1 positive

rows.study: Kawanishi M, Abo H, Ozawa M, et al. Antimicrob Agents Chemother 2017;61(1):e02057-16

primary.evidence: abstract: mcr-1 detected in 39 of 9,306 E. coli strains from the JVARM system

rows.study: Walkty A, Karlowsky JA, Adam HJ, et al. CMAJ Open 2016;4(4):E641-E645

primary.evidence: abstract: 5571 E. coli clinical isolates; 2 (0.04%) harboured mcr-1

rows.study: Treilles M, Chatre P, Drapeau A, et al. Front Microbiol 2022;13:1023403 (PMC9846274)

primary.evidence: abstract + full text: 65/1561 breeding-animal samples + 84/140 fattening = 149/1701; full text: 'All 149 mcr-1-positive isolates were characterized'

rows.verdict: denominator matches, numerator does NOT: the seed shows 49 where the primary reports 149 (a dropped leading digit); 49/1701 = 2.88% vs the primary's 149/1701 = 8.76%

rows.study: Ewers C, Goepel L, Prenger-Berninghoff E, et al. Front Microbiol 2022;13:1076315 (PMC9780603)

primary.evidence: full-text Table 1, Germany 2010-2017 cell: 6,158 isolates, 707 mcr-1 (11.5%), 2 mcr-2

rows.verdict: denominator matches, numerator and printed percentage do NOT: the seed shows 709 and 10.42% where the primary table shows 707 and 11.5%

anomalies_resolved.fix: use 707/6,158 = 11.5%; neither the seed's numerator nor its printed prevalence is the primary's

anomalies_resolved.seed: Spain 28 isolates / 17 positive / 60.7%, byte-identical to Portugal 28/17/60.7%
anomalies_resolved.primary: Ewers 2022 Table 1: Portugal 28/17/60.7% is correct; Spain is 28/16/57.1% (with 1 mcr-2)
anomalies_resolved.fix: the seed's Spain row is Portugal's row duplicated; the primary's Spain is 28/16 = 57.1%

harmonisation_columns.detection_method: molecular (whole-plasmid sequencing, subcloning, PCR) - gene-first on all isolates
harmonisation_columns.sampling_design: cross-sector convenience: commensal E. coli from farm animals + raw meat + hospital inpatients

harmonisation_columns.detection_method: molecular (real-time PCR) - gene-first on all isolates
harmonisation_columns.sampling_design: isolate screen across 20 provinces; farm animals dominant + human and pet faecal samples

harmonisation_columns.detection_method: molecular (gene screen) - gene-first on all isolates
harmonisation_columns.sampling_design: national routine veterinary AMR surveillance (JVARM), healthy food-producing animals
convenience archive of diagnostic porcine isolates, mostly Germany; a second arm screened only colistin-non-susceptible isolates
targeted farm survey: 80 breeding + 5 fattening goat farms, convenience not national surveillance

harmonisation_columns.detection_method: phenotypic (broth microdilution) then PCR only on the colistin-resistant subset - phenotype-first
harmonisation_columns.sampling_design: national sentinel-hospital surveillance (CANWARD), consecutive clinical isolates, 1 per patient per site

note: The four rows with gene-first detection (1, 6, 13, 17a) and the one phenotype-first row (28) are not methodologically comparable: a phenotype-first design can only find mcr in isolates already resistant to colistin, so it reports a floor, while gene-first designs screen every isolate for the gene.
